Iran: Demands First, Hormuz Second 🛳


Iran said that any deal with Oman on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz would not lead to the waterway being fully reopened and that the route would remain closed until the United States agreed to demands including lifting a naval blockade.

The comments were the latest sign that Iran sees its grip on the strait — which has driven up global energy prices, creating a political headache for Trump — as its best form of leverage in negotiations with Washington.

Esmail Baghaei, spokesman for the Iranian Foreign Ministry, said at a news conference on Monday that the focus of the talks with Oman was “on reaching an understanding over a route for the safe passage of shipping,” Iranian state media reported.

The Oman talks were proceeding smoothly, Baghaei added, according to the reports, but “this issue is separate from the discussion of reopening the Strait of Hormuz,” which was “contingent upon the removal of the conditions that have been imposed on the Islamic Republic of Iran” by the United States.

The US and Iran are not negotiating directly, although Secretary of State Marco Rubio said last week that the talks between Iran and Oman were being conducted with American input.

The Strait of Hormuz, which runs between Iran and Oman, is a key route for the oil and gas trade. Tehran effectively closed the waterway after the United States and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran in late February, and it has become a key sticking point as Iran and the United States alternate between periods of negotiation and bursts of fighting.

The closure of the waterway has increased energy costs in the United States, where polls show that support for the already unpopular conflict is falling. 

Hard-liners in Iran believe that the country’s ability to close it to traffic has put it in a position of strength and that it should not make diplomatic concessions.

Last week, a top Iranian national security official issued a set of demands that are part of Iran’s longstanding public negotiating stance and that he said the United States must meet before Tehran would fully reopen the waterway.

Those included the lifting of the US naval blockade and sanctions on Iran, the withdrawal of American forces from around the country, the payment of war reparations, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and the end of attacks on Iran’s allies in the region.

Most of those demands were detailed in a cease-fire agreement, known as the Islamabad Memorandum, that the United States and Iran signed in June, though that document said sanctions would be fully lifted only in the event of a final deal regarding Iran’s nuclear program.

The June agreement quickly fell apart, and most of its terms were violated within weeks.

Trump has declared the deal “over.” On Sunday, he said that economic distress and high inflation in Iran would eventually force Tehran to agree to a new deal. He did not threaten further military action against Iran, saying, “We are low-keying it.”

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.

The IRGC did not form an alliance with socialist/leftist students to overthrow the Shah; the broader Islamist forces under Ayatollah Khomeini did form a temporary tactical coalition with various leftist, socialist, Marxist, and nationalist groups (including student organizations) against the monarchy. The IRGC itself was created after the Shah’s fall in 1979 and became a key instrument for suppressing those same leftist groups. 
The temporary anti-Shah coalition
In the late 1970s, opposition to Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi’s authoritarian, Western-aligned monarchy united a wide range of forces that otherwise disagreed on ideology and goals:
•  Islamist networks loyal to Khomeini (clerics, bazaaris, and emerging Islamist student groups).
•  Leftist/Marxist organizations and guerrillas, including the Tudeh Party (pro-Soviet communists), the Organization of Iranian People’s Fedai Guerrillas (Marxist), the People’s Mujahedin of Iran (MEK/MKO, which mixed Islamist and leftist elements and was often labeled “Islamic Marxist”), and smaller Maoist or independent socialist groups.
•  Student movements, both domestic and the large Iranian student diaspora organizations (such as the Confederation of Iranian Students), which had strong leftist currents.
•  Nationalists and liberals (e.g., elements of the National Front).
These groups shared opposition to the Shah’s repression (via SAVAK), economic inequalities, and perceived dependence on the United States. Leftists often viewed Khomeini’s anti-imperialist rhetoric (“Great Satan” for the US) through a socialist/anti-Western lens and treated the Islamists as temporary allies or a transitional force toward a more progressive outcome—similar to how some saw bourgeois stages in other revolutions. Many leftist students and guerrillas participated in protests, strikes, and the final street fighting in February 1979 that helped topple the monarchy. 
Khomeini’s circle used this broad support. Leftist organizations generally backed the early referendums establishing the Islamic Republic and did not mount a strong independent challenge while the common enemy (the Shah) remained.
Formation of the IRGC and the turn against the left
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC, or Pasdaran) was established in the weeks and months after the February 1979 victory (formalized around April–May 1979). It grew out of pro-Khomeini revolutionary committees (komitehs), militias, and volunteers loyal to the emerging theocratic leadership. Its purpose was to defend the new Islamic order, counter residual Shah loyalists, and—critically—prevent other revolutionary factions (especially leftists and nationalists) from seizing or sharing power. It answered to Khomeini rather than the provisional government. 
Once the Shah was gone, the tactical alliance rapidly collapsed:
•  Islamists consolidated control through institutions, the constitution embedding velayat-e faqih (guardianship of the jurist), and parallel power structures.
•  Universities, where leftist student groups (Fedai-linked, MEK-linked, Tudeh-linked, etc.) had strong presence, became a major battleground. In 1980 Khomeini launched a “Cultural Revolution” that closed universities, purged leftist faculty and students, and installed Islamist control.
•  The IRGC, along with Hezbollah-style street enforcers and revolutionary courts, disarmed independent militias, closed leftist presses, attacked demonstrations and headquarters, and suppressed workers’ councils (shoras).
•  Armed clashes escalated, especially with the MEK after mid-1981. Thousands of leftists were arrested, tortured, or executed in waves of repression (notably 1981–1983). The Tudeh Party was banned in 1983 after forced televised confessions. Many survivors fled into exile or went underground.

On the 31st anniversary of Operation Storm, we spoke with Bojan Vulin at the bombed Iriški Venac television tower in Serbia about a history that remains very much alive here.

NATO bombed Yugoslavia for 78 days in 1999. Bridges, schools, hospitals, infrastructure and state television were struck. More than a quarter-century later, the scars remain.

Standing beneath Iriški Venac, we discussed the parallels Serbs see between what was done to their country and the opening days of the war against Iran, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and state media.

The tower itself is perhaps the most powerful metaphor. NATO bombed it, but it never fell.

It is damaged. It is scarred. And 27 years later, it is still standing.

So are the Serbian people.

Twin Lagoon, Philippines

If there’s a place where water murmurs ancient secrets to the cliffs, it’s Twin Lagoon in Coron. Nestled between towering limestone walls and cradled by the hush of the jungle, these twin emerald pools are nature’s quiet masterpiece.

The wonder is in the contrast — warm seawater merging with cool freshwater, creating an otherworldly sensation as you drift between them. At high tide, you slip through a narrow cleft in the rock; at low tide, a simple wooden ladder helps you cross above.

This isn’t just swimming — it’s a journey into stillness. Twin Lagoon doesn’t shout. It doesn’t have to. It simply opens its arms and invites you to float, breathe, and lose yourself in the moment.
